      <title>Four takeaways from Anthropic’s potentially record-breaking stock market filing</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/26/anthropic-stock-market-filing-takeaways</link>
      <description><p>The AI company’s first public financial disclosures reveal explosive growth, huge costs and risks ranging from cyber-attacks to the limits of safeguards</p><p>Anthropic <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/26/anthropic-files-listing-stock-market">has filed</a> to go public on the US stock market, revealing for the first time the AI research lab’s financials and all the risks – more than 90 pages of them – that might negatively affect its business.</p><p>The company’s investor prospectus, released on Monday, veers from hyperbolic predictions about AI’s “incredible potential” to existential risks of the technology to the reality of its current business: explosive but incredibly expensive growth. The filing to US financial regulators, known as an S-1, provides the public’s first look at an audited version of Anthropic’s finances.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/26/anthropic-stock-market-filing-takeaways">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Republican senator faces critical re-election battle in state where president’s trade war has outraged voters </p><p>Donald Trump dropped some of the US’s tariffs on Canada on Friday to “better serve the public interest” the White House said, handing a win to Susan Collins, the embattled Republican senator for Maine, as she faces a tight re-election campaign that will help determine whether Democrats can flip control of Congress.</p><p>Collins announced that the exemptions would apply to nine agricultural products, including blueberries, potatoes, apples and seaweed.
